error_description: The student applied whole-number additive arithmetic to fraction situations by adding the denominators when combining two unit fractions.
example: When asked what fraction two 1/7 pieces (4-sticks) would make together, the student answered 'One-fourteenth... because you add one-seventh and another seventh it makes 14.'

error_description: A student interprets a fraction of a partitioned whole purely by counting parts and pieces without being able to recognize the commensurate unit fraction due to a lack of recursive partitioning operations.
example: When asked what the share of 3 people is out of 27 pieces, Laura argued it is 3/27 and could not see it as 1/9 because she relied on counting 3 people out of 27 pieces.

error_description: The student proposed partitioning parts into an arbitrary number of smaller parts without anticipating whether the resulting total number of parts would allow him to produce the target fraction.
example: When trying to make a 5/5-bar into a 4/4-bar, Carlos suggested partitioning each fifth into two parts, which would only make 10 parts total.
mathematical_subtopic: coordinating two fractions in the same bar

error_description: The student experiences severe cognitive and energetic depletion when asked to coordinate two different quantities involving improper fractions.
example: Bridget was unable to operate on a problem asking how long it would take a runner to run 13/8 of a mile if 1 mile takes 6 minutes.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students misplace addition and multiplication operations when attempting to reconstruct the fraction addition algorithm, such as multiplying the numerators and adding the denominators.
authors: Shlomo Vinner, Rina Hershkowitz and Maxim Bruckheimer
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students inappropriately apply rules for whole numbers to fraction symbols, mistakenly concluding that a larger denominator indicates a larger fractional quantity.
example: When asked to compare 1/6 and 1/8, a student answered 'One eighth is bigger' and explained, '[Eight] is a bigger number I think. [Eight] is bigger than [six].'
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When mentally calculating the sum of two fractions, students may inappropriately add the numerators together and find the average of the denominators to create the new fraction.
example: To estimate 12/13 + 7/8, a student added the numerators to get 19, then found common multiples for denominators (26 and 24), averaged them to 25, and provided an estimate of 19/25.
authors: Robert E. Reys, Barbara J. Reys, Nobuhiko Nohda, Junichi Ishida, Shigeo Yoshikawa and Katsuhiko Shimizu
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students inappropriately generalize whole number operations to fraction computations by independently adding, subtracting, or multiplying numerators and denominators, or by multiplying a whole number by both parts of a fraction.
example: For 6 x 4/7, students incorrectly chose 24/42. For 3/4 - 1/6, students answered 2/2. For 5/6 + 3/4, students selected 8/10.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education. Monograph

error_description: Students incorrectly apply additive or isolated multiplicative rules, creating syntactic errors, rather than proportionally coordinating equivalent fractions on a number line.
example: When asked to find an equivalent fraction for 5/3 in twelfths on a number line, a student reasoned '6 + 6 = 12 so 8 + 8 = 16' or another reasoned '3 x 2 = 6 so 8 x 2 = 16' and incorrectly marked 16/3.
authors: George W. Bright, Merlyn J. Behr, Thomas R. Post and Ipke Wachsmuth
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: The student represents and understands the fraction 1/2 not as a fractional quantity (one out of two total pieces), but as the act of partitioning or the balance between parts, omitting any shading.
example: When asked to draw 1/2, students drew shapes partitioned down the middle but omitted standard shading, explaining it using a chopping gesture or stating 'it's cut in half, and there is two.'
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When estimating fraction addition or subtraction, students may avoid finding common denominators by incorrectly adding or subtracting directly across the numerators and denominators.
example: To estimate 12/31 - 5/8, a student subtracted the numerators (12-5) and denominators (31-8) to get 7/23.
authors: Sheri A. Hanson and Thomas P. Hogan
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly apply whole number ordering rules to fractions, judging a fraction with a larger denominator as greater because its integer is larger.
example: A student states 'One fifth is less ... because five is less than nine.'
authors: Thomas R. Post, Ipke Wachsmuth, Richard Lesh and Merlyn J. Behr
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When finding a fraction of a fraction, students rely strictly on the number of parts (e.g., 2/3 is simply '2 out of 3 pieces') and ignore remainder pieces if the grouping doesn't come out evenly, failing to repartition the unit.
example: When finding 2/3 of 9/10, Lisa grouped pieces into threes and took two from each group, stating, 'If it doesn't come out even, I pretend (the remaining) pieces are not there.'
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students attempt to estimate the sum of two fractions using a reference point but misjudge the sizes of the fractions due to a lack of understanding of fraction equivalence and order.
example: Jessie incorrectly reasoned that 5/6 is 'less than a half', leading to an incorrect estimation of the sum.
authors: Merlyn J. Behr, Ipke Wachsmuth and Thomas R. Post
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: A student treats the denominator of a fraction as a direct indicator of absolute magnitude or quantity, failing to recognize the inverse relationship between the denominator and the unit fraction size.
example: Alan concluded that a 1/8-full packet of M&Ms contained more than a 1/4-full packet because 'there's eight in here, and there's four in each of those'.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students compare fractions using fractional terms but fail to account for differences in the size of the whole units.
example: You'd get the same amount, because they're both one-half
authors: Barbara E. Armstrong and Carol Novillis Larson
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: The student teacher confuses representations for multiplication of fractions with those for division of fractions, demonstrating a rote rather than conceptual understanding of the topic.
example: When attempting to visually explain 3/4 divided by 1/2 to her class using a drawing of a wall, the teacher inadvertently modeled 1/2 of 3/4 (multiplication) rather than division.
grade_band_as_declared: seniors in an elementary teacher education program
authors: Hilda Borko, Margaret Eisenhart, Catherine A. Brown, Robert G. Underhill, Doug Jones and Patricia C. Agard
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: A student identifies fractions solely by the total number of pieces rather than relative size to the whole, demonstrating difficulty with fractional language.
example: When asked what remains if 2/7 is removed from a 7/7 bar, Josh answers 'five pieces' and guesses 'five sevenths', 'fifty sevenths', or 'seven fifths'.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: A student may be unable to calculate a fraction of a whole number if the task is posed abstractly, lacking a cue to the bar-partitioning activity through which they originally developed the concept.
example: When asked 'What is five fourteenths of 322?', Kylie responded 'Nope' when asked if she had any idea how to do it, despite successfully doing similar calculations in prior sessions.
authors: Martin A. Simon, Nicora Placa, and Arnon Avitzur
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: When comparing two fractions that are each one piece away from the whole, students misapply an additive rule, incorrectly claiming the fractions are equal because the absolute difference between the numerator and denominator is the same.
example: When comparing 4/5 and 11/12, a student incorrectly concluded they are equal, explaining 'They are equal because 5 is one more than 4 and 12 is 1 more than 11.'
authors: Kathleen A. Cramer, Thomas R. Post, and Robert C. delMas
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students rely exclusively on the size of the denominator to compare fractions, assuming that more pieces automatically means a smaller fraction regardless of the numerator.
example: When comparing 2/5 and 3/7, a student reasoned that 3/7 is smaller because 'When you use sevenths, there are more pieces, so they are smaller.'
authors: Donald M. Peck and Stanley M. Jencks
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly compare the sizes of fractional parts when the denominators are the same by inverting the relation between numerator and denominator.
example: Nine thirteenths is less than four thirteenths because "four pieces are so big, nine pieces would have to be smaller to fit the whole."
authors: Merlyn J. Behr, Ipke Wachsmuth, Thomas R. Post and Richard Lesh
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students erroneously judge two identical fractions as representing the exact same quantity without considering the size of the original reference whole, a misconception exacerbated by textbooks that present fractions without contexts.
example: Students end up putting 'equal' when asked to compare 'half' and 'half', without realizing that half of a small cookie is not the same as half of a large cookie.
journal: Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

error_description: Students confuse the operations of dividing by a whole number and dividing by a unit fraction.
example: When determining 1/2 of 2/4, Gabby was unsure whether she was dividing by 2 or dividing by 1/2.
mathematical_subtopic: Division by a whole number vs fraction
authors: Victoria R. Jacobs, Susan B. Empson

error_description: Students treat the numerals in fraction representations as whole numbers, applying whole-number schemes instead of conceptualizing the multiplicative relations between quantities.
authors: Geoffrey B. Saxe, Ronli Diakow, Maryl Gearhart

error_description: Students misapply formal properties by assuming that division is a commutative operation.
example: Performing 15:5 instead of 5:15, arguing that division is commutative.

error_description: Students map visual features to mathematical concepts based on incidental, surface-level similarities rather than conceptually relevant features, leading to incorrect connections.
authors: Martina A. Rau, Percival G. Matthews

error_description: Students incorrectly named a fractional part based on the total number of pieces in the physical model without referencing the assigned value of the whole.
example: When a train of yellow and light green rods was given the value of 'two', students named a single red rod 'one fourth' simply because four red rods made up the train, ignoring that the train represented two wholes.
authors: Elena P. Steencken, Carolyn A. Maher

error_description: Preservice teachers may incorrectly believe that valid mathematical operations, such as creating equivalent fractions with a common numerator, are mathematically 'illegal' simply because they were only explicitly taught to find common denominators.
example: When comparing 5/12 and 30/71, Jennifer's first instinct was to multiply 5/12 by 6 to get 30/72, but she hesitated, stating 'I've only been taught that you can find common denominators, so I just think that that's a wrong step to do.'
authors: Ian Whitacre, Şebnem Atabaş, Kelly Findley

error_description: Preservice teachers' intuitive drawings for measurement division can lead them to generate number sentences that reflect repeated addition or multiplication, causing a failure to recognize the overarching division structure of the problem.
example: For the measurement division problem 7 / 1/4, Jacky drew 7 rectangles each divided into 4 parts and wrote 7 x 4 = 28, struggling to connect her drawing to the concept of division.
authors: Helena P. Osana, Diana A. Royea

error_description: In continuous settings without predefined discrete pieces, students may form a 'unit fraction' by arbitrarily cutting off a remaining piece or empirically estimating a smaller size, rather than systematically equipartitioning the whole.
example: Given a continuous strip labeled 3/5, Dylan made a copy, visually estimated a 2/5 piece to add, and then tried to iterate a 'cut-off' piece as 1/5, struggling when it did not fit exactly twice into his 2/5 strip.

error_description: Students inappropriately apply whole number logic to fraction denominators, incorrectly concluding that a larger denominator makes the fraction larger.
example: A student stated 'the bigger the numerator . . . the bigger the denominator' when trying to explain why 5/7 is bigger than 1/7, reflecting the theorem-in-action 'The bigger the denominator the bigger the fraction'.

error_description: Students overgeneralize their iterative way of operating with unit fractions to non-unit fractions, producing incorrect amounts by iterating a composite unit rather than iterating the unit fraction.
example: When given a 1-rod representing 1/7 and asked to show 2/7, Isaac pulled out seven 2-rods and lined them up, stating 'it fits in there twice' instead of taking two 1-rods.

error_description: Students misapplied whole number reasoning to the denominators of unit fractions, concluding that a fraction with a larger denominator is the larger fraction.
example: Student 4 explained that one-third is bigger than one-half because 'Three is higher than two.'

error_description: When asked to find an original whole given a piece that represents a multiple of that whole, students without a splitting operation will inappropriately iterate the given piece rather than partitioning it to find the iterable unit.
example: When told a given stick is 5 times as long as another stick and asked to draw the other stick, students without splitting operations will sometimes iterate the given stick instead of positing a piece that reproduces it.

error_description: The student incorrectly associated the operation of taking a fraction of a quantity with subtraction rather than multiplication.
example: Barbara associated 'taking a fraction of something' with subtraction. For instance, she thought that 1/3 of 2/3 would be 1/3.

error_description: When faced with tasks requiring the creation of a unit fraction from a whole, students who have not yet constructed a partitive unit fraction scheme may ignore the fractional language, initially drawing a segment the same length as the given whole.
example: When asked to draw a stick 1/7 as long as a given stick, both Cody and Devin initially responded by drawing a stick the exact same length as the given stick.

error_description: The student believed that cutting the excess off an over-estimated repeated part successfully produced "one-half," failing to recognize the logical necessity that the two parts must be of equal size.
example: Jerry drew an estimate of a half-stick, repeated it to form a two-part stick, saw it was longer than the original stick, and broke off the excess part, explicitly claiming that both the original estimate and the shorter cut piece were "half."

error_description: Preservice teachers may correctly represent fraction operations pictorially but fail to connect those drawn fractional parts to the whole number quantities they represent, losing track of what dollar amount corresponds to which drawn section.
example: Tony correctly determined the dollar values for the first three fractions but in the last step erroneously thought that 1/6 of the total is $125 when 5/6 equals $750, failing to keep track of the whole numbers represented by his diagram.
authors: Jae M. Baek, Megan H. Wickstrom, Jennifer M. Tobias, Amanda L. Miller, Elif Safak, Nicole Wessman-Enzinger, J. Vince Kirwan

error_description: Students operating with the first multiplicative concept (MC1) add fractional parts by summing the number of parts regardless of their relative size.
example: In adding one-half and one-fourth, Tim said the answer would be one-fifth because one-half was one part and one-fourth was four parts, for a total of five parts.

error_description: Students may initially view wholes as indivisible when dealing with division problems with remainders, preferring to leave leftover items unshared rather than partitioning them into fractional parts.
example: When asked to share 13 cookies among 4 people, Stu dealt out 12 cookies and stated the 13th cookie would just be 'one left over. One remaining,' initially refusing to partition it.
authors: Jessica H. Hunt, Arla Westenskow, Juanita Silva, Jasmine Welch-Ptak

error_description: A student who can use distributive partitioning for equal sharing of whole items may fail to apply it when taking a fraction of a non-unit fraction because they assimilate the task into recursive partitioning, which cannot evaluate the size of a subpart of a multi-part unit.
example: When asked to show 2/5 x 3/7 using JavaBars, Kylie could not figure out how to divide 2 parts into 7 subparts, despite previously successfully sharing 11 whole bars of chocolate among 17 friends.
authors: Martin A. Simon, Melike Kara, Nicora Placa

error_description: The student conflated overlapping fractional parts when joining them, mistakenly double-counting the overlapping complement piece.
example: Jason counted twelve total parts but stated the sum of 1/4 and 1/3 was 'eight twelfths' by mistakenly including the complement of the 1/4 bar in the 1/3 bar twice.

error_description: Students may struggle to conceive of a fraction as a number with multiple equivalent names because they process fractions additively rather than multiplicatively, preventing them from holding the part-whole relationship at two hierarchical levels simultaneously.
example: A fourth grader correctly identified a partitioned sector of a circle as 'three-twelfths' and the unpartitioned equivalent sector as 'one-fourth', but when asked for another name for the one-fourth piece, the child said 'No'.

error_description: The student inappropriately generalizes whole-number division algorithms to solve non-unit fraction problems, such as dividing the total amount by the numerator or dividing the denominator by the numerator.
example: When asked what two-thirds means in the context of finding a fraction of six sweets, Rachel replied 'Twos into the number?', applying a whole-number division rule rather than partitioning.

error_description: Students misinterpret formal fraction notation when applied to an area model, conflating the written denominator or numerator directly with the absolute number of shaded parts.
example: When working with a 12-square rectangle, Stefan writes '1/4' to mean that 4 squares in the rectangle are marked, and '1/10' to mean that 10 squares are marked.

error_description: Pupils over-rely on visually checking for shape congruency to determine fractions, applying rigid 'no-no reasoning' where they falsely assume that if the visual parts of a whole are not congruent, the highlighted part cannot represent a specific unit fraction.
example: In a grid-based problem where a border is shaded, 44 pupils reasoned that 'the parts are not equal in size' so the shading couldn't be one-third, failing to calculate that the 32 shaded squares were exactly 1/3 of the 96 total squares.
grade_band_as_declared: fifth-grade pupils, between 10 and 11 years of age
authors: Tatjana Hodnik Cadez, Vida Manfreda Kolar

error_description: Pre-service teachers hold the misconception that fraction addition and fraction multiplication cannot be shown or explained using the same type of pictorial representation.
example: A pre-service teacher evaluates a vignette by incorrectly claiming, 'You cannot show both operations in the same representation,' revealing a lack of specific content knowledge about rectangle models.

error_description: Children face difficulties determining a fractional part of a discrete quantity due to the over-emphasis on the cardinal aspect of natural numbers in early education.
example: Coen faces some difficulties when he has to determine a fractional part of a discrete quantity. ... Taking this fact into account he must be misled, as soon as a question concerning fractions starts with: 'How many...'

error_description: Children physically cross out or strike a line through a written whole number to represent a half, attempting to symbolically capture the physical action of halving the quantity.
example: Taylor crossed out the numeral seven to show 'seven and a half', visually representing a seven cut in half rather than seven whole units plus an additional half unit.

error_description: Children draw on real-world social practices of food sharing to partition circular objects into many unequal pieces, attempting to balance visual area instead of creating mathematically equal fractional parts.
example: Ben cut a pizza into many unequal pieces and shared them as evenly by area as he could, making formal quantification of the shares impossible.
grade_band_as_declared: Year Three / third grade students (aged between 7.9 and 8.3 years)

error_description: Students overgeneralize the decimal representation of 'one-half', universally applying the symbol '0.5' to other bases regardless of whether the digit 5 is valid or meaningful in that base.
example: A student writes 'one-half' in base three as 0.5, and then calculates its value as 5 x 1/3 = 5/3.
authors: HELEN A. KHOURY AND RINA ZAZKIS

error_description: Students experience conceptual confusion regarding equivalent fractions, struggling to reconcile how 'splitting' a fraction into more pieces does not change its overall rational number value.
example: A student expresses confusion by stating 'it can split and split and still be... this is the same as this', struggling with the dual identity of a fraction as a physical object being split into smaller pieces versus a rational number that maintains the same value.

error_description: Students attempt to construct procedural rules for fraction multiplication based solely on superficial numerical patterns or analogies rather than underlying structural models.
example: A student tentatively suggests multiplying numerators by noticing a number analogy, but cannot initially justify it with the area model when challenged by a peer.

error_description: Students can mechanically execute a computational rule for multiplying fractions but fail entirely to interpret or apply the same operation when presented in a visual diagram.
example: Many students could correctly calculate 1/6 * 3/4, but when asked to shade 1/6 of a 3/4 dotted region in a circle diagram, they failed to recognize it as a multiplication exercise or execute it.

error_description: Students treat visual models like the number line not as sense-making tools, but as formalized procedures to be performed to satisfy the teacher's requirement to 'show your work.'
example: Zane and Jack correctly computed 5/6 x 4 using the standard algorithm, then constructed an incorrect number line representation, eventually adjusting their drawing to match their numerical answer rather than using the drawing to find the answer.
authors: Andrea McCloskey & Gwendolyn Lloyd & Courtney Lynch

error_description: When asked to estimate, students inappropriately attempt to mentally apply standard written exact computation algorithms rather than using estimation strategies.
example: A student mentally calculated 12/13 + 7/8 using the algorithm ({ad + bc}/bd) to get 193/104 instead of estimating each fraction to 1.
authors: BARBARA J. REYS, ROBERT E. REYS, AND ALFINIO FLORES PEÑAFIEL

error_description: Students incorrectly treat the entire visible portion of a number line or its arrows as the complete unit of 1, and inappropriately apply whole number counting schemes by counting tick marks instead of the continuous intervals.
example: When asked to place '1' on a number line that shows a longer interval, students might place '1' at the very end of the visible line, or they might determine a fraction's value by counting the number of tick marks instead of spaces.

error_description: Students place fractions on a number line at mixed-number positions.
example: Placing 3/5 at 3.5 or 5 3/5 on number line 0 to 5.

error_description: Learners treat the numerator and denominator as independent whole numbers, which leads to incorrect ordering and computing by adding or subtracting numerators and denominators separately.
example: Computing by adding or subtracting the numerators and denominators separately.

error_description: Students struggle to conceive a part of a whole as a relative size that can be iterated unrestrictedly, instead treating it as a discrete physical piece of an object limited by the number of original partitions.
example: Conceiving 1/3 of a circle as an actual physical piece of the represented circle rather than an area of relative size that can be iterated beyond the whole.
authors: Jose Luis Cortina & Jana Visnovska & Claudia Zuniga

error_description: A mathematically talented student experiences a severe cognitive block and emotional depletion when attempting to solve complex fraction relationships because she lacks visual or private imagery for fractions and resists drawing pictures, relying instead on numerical computation.
example: During the Box Problem, where 3/4 dm is 2/3 of an unknown height, the student is unable to compute the answer immediately, refuses to draw a picture, repeatedly moans 'my brain's not working,' and fails to solve the problem.

error_description: Students rote apply fraction conversion procedures or incorrectly apply isolated memorized rules without conceptual understanding.
example: When asked why they use a specific procedure to find equivalent fractions, a group responded 'that's what we learned' or incorrectly claimed 'the smaller the denominator, the larger the fraction' regardless of the numerator.

error_description: Students mistakenly apply a known proportional relationship between two objects to a new whole without adjusting for the new whole's length.
example: Naming the red rod 'one-half' of the orange rod because the student knew the white rod was half of the red rod, erroneously applying that half relationship to the orange rod context.

error_description: Students fail to abstract the proportional relationship across different continuous linear contexts, treating fractions on a number line differently from fractions on a physical length model.
example: A student marks 1/3 on a number line (from 0 to 1) at a completely different proportional distance than where they would cut a piece of ribbon of the same overall length to show 1/3.
authors: Xiaofen Zhang & M. A. (Ken) Clements & Nerida F. Ellerton

error_description: Prospective teachers misorder fractions that share the same numerator, incorrectly assuming that a larger denominator correlates with a larger overall fraction size.
example: Greg incorrectly ordered 3/11, 3/14, and 3/17, struggling to maintain equal sized pieces in his mental model before wondering if a bigger denominator means a smaller value.

error_description: Pre-service teachers perform fraction division using algorithms like invert-and-multiply but treat it purely as a mechanical procedure without conceptual meaning.
example: A participant calculates 1/2 ÷ 1/3 using the invert-and-multiply algorithm but states 'for me it does not mean anything' when asked about the meaning of the expression.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Executing fraction algorithms instrumentally rather than relationally, teachers believe that multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the same number changes the value of the fraction.
example: Stating that multiplying the numerator and denominator by 2 doubles the value of the fraction.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Logical error where the meanings attributed to fractions or the addition of fractions do not make sense in daily life, such as using quantities greater than the whole.
example: First, 1/2 of the nuts in the sack were sold and then 3/4 of them were sold. What is the amount of nuts sold in total? [S7]
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students mechanically apply fraction rules without conceptual understanding, such as assuming that multiplying by the reciprocal of a proper fraction will still decrease the unit.
example: When predicting whether N divided by 11/25 is less than N, a student mentally inverts and multiplies but claims that 'multiplying fractions decreases the unit', failing to recognize that 25/11 is greater than 1.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students misinterpret the visual representation of mixed fractions in area models, perceiving fully shaded integer models as part of a compound fraction rather than a whole.
example: A student accepted an area model that represents '1 whole' divided into four equal parts as 6/4 rather than identifying the separate 1 whole of the mixed fraction 1 2/4.
authors: Fatma Gizem Karaoglan Yilmaz, Burçin Gökkurt Özdemir & Zehra Yasar
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Students select and apply an incorrect mathematical operation, such as multiplying by a fraction instead of dividing.
example: When asked to evaluate 125 ÷ 1/5, the student calculates 1/5 of 125, resulting in 25.
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: When using visual or concrete grouping models to solve fraction division problems, students may misinterpret the remainder by identifying it as a fraction of the original unit rather than as a fraction of the divisor.
example: When dividing 10 yards of fabric by 3/4 of a yard to make pillowcases, a student counts 13 pillowcases and has 1/4 of a yard of fabric left over, incorrectly concluding the final answer is 13 1/4 instead of 13 1/3.
authors: Anat Klemer, Shirley Rapoport & Hanna Lev-Zamir
journal: International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology

error_description: Prospective teachers over-generalize fraction algorithms, often adding or subtracting across numerators and denominators, or incorrectly maintaining common denominators during multiplication.
example: When multiplying two fractions with a common denominator, such as 2/15 x 7/15, a PST might incorrectly keep the common denominator to get 14/15.
authors: LouAnn H. Lovin, Alexis L. Stevens, John Siegfried, Jesse L. M. Wilkins, Anderson Norton

error_description: When asked to fairly distribute items (e.g., pizzas) among groups of varying sizes, some participants fail to grasp the concept of equal distribution, meaning they distribute the items without ensuring that each individual person receives the same proportional amount.
example: some of the pilot participants would ignore this constraint [fairly distributed] as they struggled with distributing the pizzas among all 24 people... 19% of the participants could not solve the problem nor did they understand the key concept of equal distribution (that each person should receive the same amount of pizza).
authors: Helena P. Osana, Guy L. Lacroix, Bradley J. Tucker, Chantal Desrosiers

error_description: A prospective teacher lacks conceptual understanding of fraction division, relying solely on procedural steps while confusing algorithms, and attempts to use visual representations that simply illustrate final numerical answers rather than modeling the mathematical logic.
example: Vonda tries to explain division by drawing two rectangles for the dividend and a third rectangle equal to 3/4 of the area of the first two for the divisor, later quitting because she is "rusty". In another task, she draws 4 liters poured into 6 containers but artificially labels each share with the final answer of 2/3 instead of the intermediate 4/6.
authors: Charalambos Y. Charalambous, Heather C. Hill, Deborah L. Ball

error_description: When using a benchmark strategy to compare fractions, learners incorrectly assume that 'closer to the benchmark' always means 'smaller' (or larger), failing to coordinate the magnitude of the distance with the directionality relative to the benchmark (especially when both fractions are greater than the benchmark).
example: PTs incorrectly concluded that 8/9 > 12/13 by (a) correctly drawing on BV[1] to identify the distance from 1 as 1/9 and 1/13, (b) applying SNP to state that 1/9 > 1/13, but then (c) incorrectly concluding from this that 8/9 > 12/13... Many PTs argued that one fraction was larger than another because 'it was closer to 1.' While this reasoning is valid when comparing fractions both <1, it is not when comparing fractions that are both greater than a benchmark, such as 1.
authors: Eva Thanheiser, Dana Olanoff, Amy Hillen, Ziv Feldman, Jennifer M. Tobias, Rachael M. Welder

error_description: A student incorrectly adds fractions by treating them as whole numbers, adding the numerators together and adding the denominators together.
example: When calculating 1/3 + 1/2, the student adds the numerators (1+1=2) and denominators (3+2=5) to get 2/5.

error_description: A student finds a fraction between two given fractions by incorrectly choosing a numerator between the given numerators and a denominator between the given denominators.
example: A student answered that 2/3 is between 1/2 and 3/4 'because 2 is between the 1 and the 3, and on the bottom the 3 lies between the 2 and the 4'.
authors: TIM ROWLAND, PETER HUCKSTEP and ANNE THWAITES

error_description: When sharing multiple wholes, learners and teachers exhibit ambiguity regarding the referent unit, confusing the fractional amount relative to a single whole with the fractional amount relative to the entire collection of wholes.
example: When examining a student's answer of 'one third' for sharing 2 pizzas among 3 friends, a teacher points out the ambiguity by asking, 'One third of what?'
authors: P. Holt Wilson, Paola Sztajn, Cyndi Edgington, Jere Confrey

error_description: A student incorrectly compares two fractions using a diagram by treating the number of pieces shaded as whole numbers, ignoring the relationship to the whole.
example: "In the two sets above you can see that 7 pieces is greater than 6 pieces, so 7/8 is larger than 6/7."
mathematical_subtopic: number of pieces vs fraction size
authors: Tonya Gau Bartell • Corey Webel • Brian Bowen • Nancy Dyson

error_description: Students perform operations incorrectly on word problems because they misunderstand the mathematical language, confusing what information is given with what is being asked.
example: In a problem stating 'she gave 1/2 of it, which was 1 3/4 lt', the student fails to understand the hidden statement that half of the original quantity is 1 3/4, leading to an incorrect operation.

error_description: When comparing fractions with a common numerator, a student mistakenly concludes that the fraction with the larger denominator is the greater fraction, misapplying whole number magnitude logic.
example: When comparing 6/14 and 6/15, the student incorrectly states that 6/15 is larger 'Because 15 is greater than 14.'
authors: Meghan Shaughnessy, Timothy A. Boerst, Susanna Owens Farmer

error_description: Students arbitrarily map numbers from a word problem into a fraction's numerator and denominator without understanding the problem's context or quantities.
example: 12 candies bisect to 5 people, so everyone gets 12/5 candies.
authors: Der-Ching Yang & Iwan Andi J. Sianturi
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students erroneously subtract numerators from numerators and denominators from denominators, or fail to understand how to handle a zero in the numerator.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students specify fractional prices for individual items in a set without realizing that the sum of these fractional parts must exactly equal one whole.
example: Students priced items in a set as 1/8, 2/8, 3/8, and 4/8, not noticing until prompted that these summed to 10/8, which is more than the price of the whole set.
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students incorrectly compare fractions by employing gap thinking, where they evaluate the absolute difference between a fraction's numerator and denominator rather than their proportional relationship.
example: A student stating that 3/5 is larger than 5/8 because there is 'less of a gap' between 3 and 5 than between 5 and 8.
grade_band_as_declared: fifth, sixth, and seventh grade (middle school)
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: Students believe they can exchange fractional pieces one-to-one without considering their actual mathematical value or equivalence.
example: When asked what to exchange a one-half piece for, a student removes the one-half piece and attempts to place a single one-sixteenth piece in its place.
authors: Saeideh Heshmati & Nicole Kersting & Taliesin Sutton
journal: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education

error_description: When asked to find pairs of fractions that total a specific whole number greater than one, a student defaults to a part-whole image and provides fractions that sum to exactly one.
example: Suggesting 'two fifths and three fifths' and 'one third and two thirds' as pairs of numbers that add up to five.

error_description: Students' self-generated part-whole diagrams, typically circles, are sometimes taken too literally, which hinders their ability to conceptually access their knowledge of fractions.
authors: Jeremy Hodgen, Dietmar Küchemann, Margaret Brown and Robert Coe

error_description: Teachers view equal sharing scenarios involving whole units exclusively as division and conceptually separate from fractions, unless the sharing explicitly forces objects to be broken into smaller fractional parts.
example: Teachers rejected the problem '4 cookies shared among 4 people' because they believed 'it sounds more like division than fractions.'

error_description: Students struggle with compensation logic, failing to understand that dividing a whole into a larger number of equal parts results in smaller individual portions.
example: Children continue to struggle with this relation, for example, judging the fraction 1/6 to be larger than 1/3, and using ineffective strategies for creating partitions of the appropriate size.
authors: Rachel E. Wing, Carole R. Beal
